t: 3430 – Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subarrays
o: We need, over all subarrays of length 1..k, the sum of every subarray's maximum plus the sum of every subarray's minimum. With n up to 80000, enumerating subarrays is impossible. Classic technique: for each right endpoint i compute S(i) = sum of max over ALL subarrays ending at i using a monotonic stack, then subtract the contribution of subarrays longer than k. If h(i) = Σ_{j≤i} max(a[j..i]), then h(i) = h(prevGreaterOrEqual(i)) + a[i]·(i − prevGreaterOrEqual(i)), and bounded sum ending at i equals h(i) − h(i−k). Symmetric logic handles minima. Example: nums=[1,2,3], k=2 gives max-total 9 and min-total 11 → 20.
k: h(i) = sum of maxima of all subarrays ending at i satisfies h(i) = h(p) + a[i]*(i-p) where p is the previous strictly-greater index.
Bounded-length sums come free: g(i) = h(i) − h(i−k) drops exactly the subarrays starting before i−k+1.
Run the same routine with flipped comparisons to get the minimum totals.

a.i: A monotonic stack maintains, for each i, the previous dominant element; the difference in indices tells how many new subarrays inherit the current extremum, giving an O(1) amortized recurrence for h.
s: For maxima: keep a stack of indices with strictly decreasing values; pop while nums[top] <= nums[i].
Set h[i] = h[j] + nums[i]*(i−j) with j the new top (or −1), add h[i] − (i≥k ? h[i−k] : 0) to the answer.
Repeat with >= popped for minima; return both totals summed.
a.t: O(n) — each index is pushed/popped from the stacks at most once, twice overall.
a.sp: O(n) — the h array and stack.

w: This stack-plus-prefix-difference trick is the intended hard-part insight; mention it explicitly in interviews. Pitfall: use strict vs non-strict comparison consistently (either works here since equal elements just split contributions correctly); watch overflow (n·|value| up to 8e10) requiring 64-bit. Follow-up: extend to exactly-size-k windows (sliding deque) or sum of second maxima.
